questions.question: Rotavirus vaccines in Canada.
questions.model_answer:
a) RotaTeq (RV5) is pentavalent, containing five human-bovine reassortants expressing human outer capsid proteins G1, G2, G3, G4 and P1A[8] on a bovine WC3 backbone. Rotarix (RV1) is monovalent, G1P1A[8], and protects heterotypically against G2, G3, G4 and G9 through shared P[8] and cross-reactive immunity.

b) RotaTeq: human-bovine reassortant derived from the bovine strain WC3. Rotarix: attenuated human strain 89-12 (RIX4414), passaged in cell culture.

c) Routine immunization of all healthy infants, to be given as part of the primary infant schedule; particularly important given rotavirus is the leading cause of severe infant gastroenteritis. Also given to preterm infants who are clinically stable, and may be given to infants in hospital with appropriate contact precautions.

d) (1) Anaphylaxis to a vaccine component or a previous dose (RotaTeq contains latex in the applicator; Rotarix oral applicator is latex-containing in some presentations). (2) History of intussusception, or an uncorrected congenital malformation of the gastrointestinal tract predisposing to intussusception (e.g. Meckel diverticulum). (3) Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) — risk of prolonged vaccine-virus shedding and vaccine-associated gastroenteritis. (4) Age outside the licensed window — first dose should not be started at or after 15 weeks and no dose given after 8 months of age. Precautions: moderate to severe acute illness including acute gastroenteritis, chronic gastrointestinal disease, other immunodeficiency or immunosuppressive therapy.

e) Both are given orally only — never injected. RotaTeq: 3 doses of 2 mL at approximately 2, 4 and 6 months. Rotarix: 2 doses of 1.5 mL at approximately 2 and 4 months. For both, the first dose is given between 6 and 14 weeks 6 days of age, doses are a minimum of 4 weeks apart, and the series must be completed by 8 months of age. If a dose is regurgitated it is not repeated. The series should be completed with the same product where possible.

f) Generally well tolerated. Mild irritability, fever, vomiting and diarrhea occur slightly more often than in placebo recipients. The important adverse event is intussusception — an excess of roughly 1 to 5 cases per 100,000 vaccinated infants, concentrated in the 7 days after the first dose; this is far lower than the risk with the withdrawn rhesus reassortant vaccine RotaShield. Vaccine virus is shed in the stool for up to 2–4 weeks, with rare transmission to contacts, and can cause prolonged infection in infants with SCID.
questions.beyond_mandell: NACI rotavirus statement: first dose by 14 weeks 6 days, series completed by 8 months.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort answer says the first dose may be started at 6 weeks without an upper limit and lists RotaTeq at 2, 4 and 6 months only; NACI specifies the first dose must be given before 15 weeks (by 14 weeks 6 days) of age, with the whole series completed by 8 months.

cohort_answer.text: A) Rotateq (RV5): live attenuated pentavalent bovine-human reassortment vaccine (x3 doses), strains G1/G2/G3/G4 (human) x P7[5] (bovine), G6 (bovine) x P1[8] (human). Rotarix (RV1): live attenuated monovalent vaccine from single human strain RIX44144 (x2 doses). B) Rotateq - human-bovine reassortment (5); Rotarix - human strain only (1). C) Rotateq: 3 doses, routine, start at 6 weeks; Rotarix: 2 doses, min 4 weeks apart, start at 6 weeks; both must give last dose before 8 months. D) Serious allergy to vaccine component or previous dose; history of intussusception or greater susceptibility; known immunodeficiency (SCID); >8 months of age. Precautions: altered immunocompetence, moderate-severe illness including acute gastroenteritis, chronic GI disease. E) Rotateq: 3 oral doses at 2,4,6 months (first dose 6-12 weeks, last before 8 months, min q4 weeks); Rotarix: 2 oral doses. F) Generally well tolerated; small increased risk of intussusception, hematochezia; incidence of fever, vomiting, diarrhea ≥1% higher in vaccinees vs controls after each dose.

questions.question: Rotavirus.

parts.text: Pathogenesis of diarrhea in rotavirus infection.

parts_raw.text: A. Pathogenesis of diarrhea in rotavirus

questions.model_answer:
a) The pathogenesis is multifactorial and incompletely understood, with three complementary mechanisms: (1) Malabsorption from mucosal injury – rotavirus replicates in villous enterocytes of the small intestine, producing shortened/blunted villi, crypt hypertrophy and loss of absorptive cells with depressed disaccharidase activity, reducing glucose–sodium cotransport and increasing paracellular permeability. (2) NSP4 viral enterotoxin – the nonstructural glycoprotein NSP4 raises intracellular calcium and activates a calcium-dependent chloride channel (TMEM16A), driving a net secretory state (secretion of fluid, sodium and chloride). (3) Enteric nervous system activation – ENS-mediated secretion and intestinal hypermotility contribute to diarrhea and vomiting (attenuated experimentally by lidocaine, serotonin antagonists, and clinically by the enkephalinase inhibitor racecadotril).

b) (1) Severe combined immunodeficiency disease (SCID) – added because of prolonged vaccine-virus shedding and diarrhea in these infants. (2) History of intestinal intussusception (also an uncorrected congenital GI malformation predisposing to intussusception). A severe allergic reaction to a previous dose or vaccine component is the original contraindication.

cohort_answer.text:
A: Poorly understood. Malabsorption from mucosal damage and suppression of brush border enzymes. Enterotoxin leads to secretory state. Villi blunted and shorter

B: Hx of intussusception. Known immunodeficiency (SCID). Known hypersensitivity. Severe anaphylactic allergy
